payload.scores:
SECOND FILL. The first pass eliminated X2 on the C1 freshness veto with an unprobed claim. The claim is false; the scoring below is grounded in three probes run since.

THE PROBES THAT GROUND THIS SCORING
  run-3d8fb30546e5 — a file written to the tree and never staged: plain search exits 1 with no match; the same search with --untracked FINDS it, with its line number; context works alongside.
  run-1ae8b534b535 A/B — --untracked respects the ignore rules (a file inside an ignored dependency directory is skipped), and --no-exclude-standard reaches it. So ignore behaviour is correct by default AND controllable.
  run-1ae8b534b535 C/D — the machine-readable output shape DIFFERS between modes. Working tree: three fields, path / line / text. Ref: three fields, but the FIRST is 'ref:path' — the ref and the path share one field, joined by a colon. A path containing a colon is therefore ambiguous to a parser that splits on it.

                                 wt   X1 fit-per-job   X2 one-searcher   X3 fit + meaning
C1 freshness            VETO      —   PASS            PASS              PASS
C2 reach                VETO      —   PASS            PASS              PASS
C3 one-click install      5           4               5                 4
C4 structured output      4           5               3                 5
C5 one impl per job       5           5               5                 5
C6 bounded cost           3           4               3                 4
C7 selection correctness  5           5               5                 2
C8 no migration debt      2           3               3                 5
C9 own-failure evidence   5           5               4                 3
WEIGHTED TOTAL (C3-C9)          —   136             124               113

WHAT CHANGED FROM THE SUPERSEDED FILL, and why each moved:
  C1 for X2: FAIL → PASS. The blind spot is a default, not a property. This is the correction.
  C6 for X2: 4 → 3. Version-control grep has no built-in per-line width cap and no timeout of its own, so bounding is entirely ours at the boundary. The packaged searcher offers both natively. Still a small difference — both are bounded by us in the end — hence one point.
  C9 for X2: 2 → 4. The score of 2 was punishing X2 for contradicting a measured local failure. Once the veto claim collapsed, that contradiction was mine, not X2's. X2 now scores 4 on real positive evidence: probes P2, P3 and the three above all measure it directly, and none of them is against it. It is not 5 only because P3 recorded the ref ambiguity, which X2 leans on more heavily than X1 does.

THE SCORES THAT NOW DECIDE, since the veto no longer does.

C4 STRUCTURED OUTPUT — X1 5, X2 3, and this is where X2 genuinely pays. The packaged searcher emits typed records with line numbers, spans and submatch offsets. Version-control grep emits delimited text, and probe D showed the delimiting is not uniform across modes: the ref case packs two identifiers into the field the working-tree case uses for one. Our parser must therefore branch on mode, and the branch is exactly where a parser silently mis-reads an edge case. That is not a hypothetical risk in this project — R19 exists because a guard already blamed the wrong thing when its own parsing was off.

C3 ONE-CLICK INSTALLABILITY — X2 5, X1 4, and X2 wins it outright. X2 needs no dependency at all: version control is already a hard prerequisite of the whole system. X1 depends on a package resolving a per-platform binary, and if it ever fails to, there is NO fallback — an exposure the owner has accepted, but an exposure.

C5 — all three score 5 under the corrected definition, which is the point: C5 stopped discriminating the moment the job boundary was drawn correctly. Under its old definition it produced the entire wrong architecture by itself.

STRUCTURE METRICS
  X1: 9 elements, 14 inter-element edges, longest chain 4. Retrieval splits into a working-tree element and a record element sharing ONE addressing contract — a contract seam, which is the kind that stays stable.
  X2: 8 elements, 12 edges, chain 4. Simpler, and the simplicity is real rather than nominal — one subprocess, one parser family, one failure mode to bound.
  X3: 9 elements, 15 edges, chain 5.
  All three keep K4 and K5 adjacent, so none is scored down on the partitioning's first strong claim. All three keep F33 and F34 in one element, per the second.

THE FORMULATED EXAMPLES, WALKED AGAIN with the correction in place
  UC-B step 3 'find a fact and read the lines around it' — X1 one call, typed records. X2 one call, delimited text, and it now DOES see the agent's newly written file. Both satisfy R3; they differ in what the caller must parse.
  UC-B ext 2a 'what did a shipped iteration decide' — identical in all three; Row 2 has one surviving option.
  UC-B ext 2b 'a source outside the repository' — X1 can search a directory that is not a repository at all. X2 CANNOT: version-control grep needs a repository. This did not surface in the first walk and it is a genuine functional gap, not a preference — it maps to R7 and need N1. It does not eliminate X2, because declared external roots can be read without being searched, but it narrows what X2 delivers and M5 must weigh it.
  UC-H 'the law minted this afternoon reaches the packet' — X1 and X2 identical; X3 delivers whatever scores highest, checkable by nobody.
  UC-A ext 6a and UC-D — identical in all three.
  THE WALK'S FINDING: with the veto gone, the examples discriminate on TWO axes only — what the caller must parse, and whether a non-repository source can be searched. Everything else is shared.
payload.front:
THE NON-DOMINATED SET: {X1 fit-per-job, X2 one-searcher}. Two survivors, and neither dominates.

X1 — a packaged searcher answers the working tree, version-control grep answers the record, rules by declared applicability plus a report of unattached rules.
  Better at: structured output (typed records against delimited text whose shape shifts between modes), native bounding, and searching a source that is not a repository at all.
  Pays: one dependency that must resolve a per-platform binary, with no fallback if it does not; nine elements against eight.

X2 — version-control grep answers both, in --untracked mode for the working tree; rules as X1.
  Better at: installability — no dependency whatsoever, since version control is already a hard prerequisite; simplicity — one mechanism, one subprocess, one failure mode to bound, eight elements against nine.
  Pays: our parser must branch on mode and split a field that packs two identifiers; no native caps; and it cannot search outside a repository at all, which narrows R7.

THE TRADE, stated in one line so M5 inherits a question rather than a preference: X1 buys typed output and reach beyond the repository, at the cost of a dependency with no fallback; X2 buys zero dependencies and one moving part, at the cost of parsing risk and a narrower reach.

WHAT STAYS OPEN INSIDE BOTH SURVIVORS, so the front is not falsely tidy: the guidance selector's vocabulary — state ids, state kinds, or tags — is unresolved in both, and probe P5 measured why it is not free (ten ledger nodes carry applicability, zero machine-state nodes do, and its content is prose). That is the M5 spike, and it is orthogonal to the X1/X2 choice.

NO WINNER IS PICKED HERE. That is M5's job, and this fill exists because the first one picked one by accident, through an elimination that was never measured.
payload.eliminations:
X3 FIT-PER-JOB WITH RULES BY MEANING — ELIMINATED AS DOMINATED, unchanged from the superseded fill because its reason was never the one in question.
WHAT IT WAS BETTER AT, said first: migration cost, decisively — 5 against 3. It needs nothing rewritten and nothing authored going forward, which also means it works on rules written by someone who never heard of the selector. That is a real advantage for a method meant to be used by people who did not build it.
WHY IT LOSES: C7 selection correctness, 2 against 5, at weight 5 against C8's weight 2. Semantic selection cannot be checked — a rule scoring highly against a state's statement may still be the wrong rule, and there is no ground truth here to distinguish them. Its failure mode is a wrong selection indistinguishable from a right one, which is the same shape as every other defect this iteration has found.
I checked that no defensible weighting rescues it: X3 would need migration cost to outweigh selection correctness, which would mean caring more about not rewriting ten nodes than about whether the delivered rules are the right ones. The weights were set before any candidate was scored.
NOT DISCARDED, DEFERRED: X3's mechanism is the natural fallback if declared applicability proves too burdensome to author in practice. The M5 spike should record what X3 WOULD have selected for the same states — nearly free at spike time, impossible to reconstruct later.

RETRACTED — THE ELIMINATION OF X2, which the superseded fill recorded on the C1 freshness veto.
The claim was that version-control grep cannot see a file the agent wrote and has not staged. It is false: --untracked finds it. The claim was plausible, consequential, and never probed, in a milestone whose own earlier state exists specifically to settle claims like it against the real channel. I ran five probes two states earlier and then wrote a veto on an unprobed sixth.
The retraction stands beside the claim in the record rather than replacing it. Both fills are readable; the first is marked superseded.
WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS GATE: the eliminated candidate was the FIRST PASS'S OWN CHOICE. Eliminating it on a false claim would have produced a record in which the architecture was reversed twice on two different mistakes, and looked deliberate both times.

NOT ELIMINATED, NEVER ENUMERATED, and deliberate: a combination splitting F33 (return work) from F34 (keep the path back open) across elements. Excluded by the chart rather than scored, because this project has already run that configuration by accident and deadlocked the machine in silence. C9 is weight 5 to keep exactly that out of the space.
